title: The Visitor of the Ninth Floor
premise: Quentin Nakamura, a late-night radio host in a snowbound city, begins receiving calls from listeners who died the week before—each one asking him to pass along a message he cannot verify and cannot refuse. When a downtown excavation crew unearths a door sealed from the inside, Quentin realizes the calls are leaking from the ninth floor of the demolished Aldrich Hotel, where in 1974 something was taken from the thing that lived below. The messages trace back to a woman named Iris, the hotel's last night clerk, who hid the stolen object—her own name, written on a hotel ledger page—inside the walls. Quentin must descend through the frost-patterned ruin and return it, choosing between the belonging the visitor offers him and the duty of letting the dead stay dead. He gives the name back, the calls stop, and the final broadcast is silence that finally sounds like peace.
about_author: Quentin Sandoval is the pen name of a former overnight radio engineer who spent nine years in stations that smelled of dust and hot vacuum tubes. They write horror about people who keep records because no one else will.

chapters.title: Dead Air, Warm Voices
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. On his insomniac call-in show, Quentin takes a call from a listener who, he later confirms, died four days ago. She thanks him for playing her song and hangs up. The emotional beat is uncanny tenderness—Quentin, isolated and invisible in his own life, feels seen for the first time in years, and starts a log.

chapters.title: The Documentation Is the Prayer
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. More dead callers, each with small requests: a message, an apology, a song. Quentin transcribes everything in a ledger, treating accuracy as devotion. His station manager warns him the ratings are weirdly spiking. The beat is compulsive purpose—Quentin has found a duty, and duty feels like belonging.

chapters.title: What the Excavator Found
chapters.summary: POV Marisol, an excavation foreman whose crew uncovers a door beneath the Aldrich Hotel's ruins, its bolts turned from the inside. Frost blooms across the site in patterns too regular to be natural. Marisol calls the late-night radio station on instinct. The beat is dread—the city's past refusing to stay buried.

chapters.title: The Night Clerk, 1974
chapters.summary: POV Iris, in interlocking fragments from 1974. The Aldrich's ninth floor was never on the elevator panel, yet guests checked in. Iris, the night clerk, discovered the ledger page bearing her own name had been taken by something below, making her a guest who could never check out. The beat is tragic recognition: Quentin realizes the dead callers are all ninth-floor guests.

chapters.title: Signal Through Frost
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. The calls change: the dead now speak in unison, and the frost patterns on Marisol's site spell out Quentin's name and frequency. His manager pulls the show; Quentin broadcasts anyway from a pirate transmitter. The beat is defiance—he chooses the dead over the living world that never claimed him.

chapters.title: Marisol's Bargain
chapters.summary: POV Marisol. The visitor offers Marisol her drowned brother's voice in exchange for opening the door. She nearly accepts, hearing him sing in the frost. Quentin talks her down over the air, and the cost is immediate: the visitor takes the transmitter. The beat is love against duty—Marisol's grief weaponized, and refused.

chapters.title: The Ledger Page
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. Following Iris's messages, Quentin finds her hidden confession in the station's founding archives: the stolen name was sealed inside the old transmitter housing, sold to the station in 1974. He has been broadcasting through it all along. The beat is horrified clarity—his sanctuary was always the visitor's instrument.

chapters.title: Ninth Floor
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. Descending through the excavation at night, Quentin crosses the frost-written threshold into the preserved ninth floor, where the dead guests wait in the lobby, patient and kind. The visitor, wearing Iris's face, offers him a room, a name, a place to belong forever. The beat is seduction—every lonely year answered at once.

chapters.title: Return What Was Taken
chapters.summary: POV Quentin, climax. Quentin finds the ledger page inside the transmitter's heart and understands the trap: returning it means Iris's name is no longer his to keep, and the visitor will have no claim on him—or anyone. Iris herself appears, asking him to finish it. He reads her name back into the ledger. The floor begins to let its guests go.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: POV Quentin, resolution. The ninth floor collapses into clean snow; the dead callers' final calls are goodbyes, each one grateful. Marisol fills the site, and Quentin hosts one last broadcast with no callers at all. He signs off with Iris's song. The beat is earned peace—belonging found not in being kept, but in being released.
